column1: 41:1|In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, a man of royal descent and one of the king's officers, came to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah with ten men. They shared a meal there at Mizpah.|Keeps royal ancestry, office, ten men, and the shared meal before the attack.

41:2|Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword. Ishmael killed the man the king of Babylon had appointed over the land.|Keeps the group's attack followed by Ishmael's singular killing of the appointed governor.

41:3|Ishmael also killed all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, along with the Chaldean soldiers found there.|Distinguishes the Judeans from the occupying soldiers without supplying numbers.
41:4|The day after Gedaliah was killed, before anyone knew about it,|Lets the temporal introduction continue into the arriving pilgrims.

41:5|eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria. Their beards were shaved, their clothes torn, and their bodies cut. They carried a grain offering and frankincense to bring to the house of the **LORD**.|Preserves all places, eighty men, mourning injuries, and offerings without explaining away the ruined sanctuary.

41:6|Ishmael son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he walked. When he reached them, he said, “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.”|Keeps Ishmael's tears as narrated without labeling his motive.

41:7|Once they were inside the town, Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and threw them into the cistern.|Makes the compressed slaughter-into-cistern construction intelligible without softening it.

41:8|But ten of them said to Ishmael, “Don't kill us! We have stores hidden in the fields: wheat, barley, oil, and honey.” So he held back and did not kill them with the others.|Retains all stored commodities and the ten men's escape from the massacre.

41:9|The cistern where Ishmael threw the bodies of the men he had killed alongside Gedaliah was the one King Asa had made because of Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.|Keeps the difficult association with Gedaliah and the cistern's history; note explains the uncertain phrase.

41:10|Ishmael took captive all the people left in Mizpah: the king's daughters and everyone else whom Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. Ishmael son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.|Retains royal daughters and the repeated captivity verb as the situation worsens.
41:11|Johanan son of Kareah and all the army commanders with him heard about all the evil Ishmael son of Nethaniah had done.|Keeps the narrator's judgment and the commanders' response to news.

41:12|They gathered all their men and set out to fight Ishmael son of Nethaniah. They found him by the great pool at Gibeon.|Reads the many waters as a large pool, identifying the location without modern reconstruction.
41:13|When all the people with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and the army commanders with him, they were glad.|Preserves the captives' emotional response before their movement.
41:14|All those Ishmael had taken captive from Mizpah turned around and went back to Johanan son of Kareah.|Makes the change of allegiance and direction readable without adding combat.
41:15|But Ishmael son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men and went to the Ammonites.|Retains eight survivors without inventing the fate of the other two.

41:16|Johanan son of Kareah and all the army commanders with him gathered the people he had recovered from Ishmael son of Nethaniah after the murder of Gedaliah son of Ahikam: the men of war, women, children, and eunuchs taken from Mizpah and brought back from Gibeon.|Unpacks the long recovery clause while preserving all groups and both places.
41:17|They went and stayed at Geruth-chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go on into Egypt,|Follows the read form Chimham and retains the stopping place as a name.

41:18|away from the Chaldeans. They were afraid of them because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had killed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land.|Keeps the reason for fear as the group's expectation, not a reported reprisal.

42:1|Then all the army commanders, Johanan son of Kareah, Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people, from the least to the greatest, came forward.|Preserves Jezaniah here rather than harmonizing the name with 43:2.

42:2|They said to Jeremiah the prophet, “Please hear our plea. Pray to the **LORD** your God for us, for all this remnant. Once we were many; now only a few of us are left, as you can see.|Preserves your God and the contrast between former numbers and the remnant.
42:3|May the **LORD** your God show us the way to go and what we should do.”|Keeps the twofold request for direction and action.

42:4|Jeremiah the prophet answered, “I hear you. I will pray to the **LORD** your God as you ask. Everything the **LORD** tells me in answer to you, I will tell you. I will hold nothing back.”|Retains both divine names and Jeremiah's promise of a complete answer.

42:5|They said to Jeremiah, “May the **LORD** be a true and faithful witness against us if we fail to do everything the **LORD** your God sends you to tell us.|Maintains the self-binding witness formula rather than weakening it to good intentions.

42:6|Whether it is welcome or unwelcome, we will obey the **LORD** our God, to whom we are sending you. Then things will go well for us, because we obey the **LORD** our God.”|Renders good or bad as the hearers' reception and preserves the switch to our God.
42:7|Ten days later, the word of the **LORD** came to Jeremiah.|Retains the waiting interval without explanation.
42:8|He called Johanan son of Kareah, all the army commanders with him, and all the people, from the least to the greatest.|Repeats the full audience so the answer matches the request.
42:9|He told them, “This is what the **LORD**, the God of Israel, says—the one you sent me to with your plea:|Links the answer explicitly to their commission.

42:10|‘If you will stay in this land, I will build you up and not tear you down; I will plant you and not uproot you. For I have relented over the disaster I brought on you.|Preserves building and planting motifs and divine relenting without a doctrinal gloss.

42:11|Do not fear the king of Babylon, whom you now fear. Do not fear him, declares the **LORD**, for I am with you to save you and rescue you from his hand.|Keeps the repeated prohibition and the hand image.
42:12|I will grant you mercy, so that he will have mercy on you and restore you to your own ground.’|Retains the king as the second agent of mercy and the restoration wording.
42:13|“But if you say, ‘We will not stay in this land,’ and refuse to obey the **LORD** your God,|Keeps the condition running across verses.

42:14|if you say, ‘No! We will go to Egypt, where we will see no war, hear no trumpet, and go hungry for no bread. That is where we will live,’|Retains all three imagined freedoms as the people's speech.

42:15|then hear the word of the **LORD**, remnant of Judah. This is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you are determined to enter Egypt and settle there,|Expresses setting the face as determination while retaining the two divine names.
42:16|the sword you fear will catch up with you there in Egypt. The famine you dread will cling to you there in Egypt. There you will die.|Preserves the personified pursuit and repeated location.

42:17|Everyone determined to go and settle in Egypt will die by sword, famine, or plague. No survivor or fugitive will escape the disaster I am bringing on them.’|Retains the three threats and paired denial of escape.

42:18|“For this is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘As my anger and wrath were poured out on Jerusalem's inhabitants, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you enter Egypt. You will become an example invoked in oaths, an object of horror, a curse, and a disgrace. You will never see this place again.’|Keeps the poured wrath and four consequences, explaining the oath term in context.
42:19|“The **LORD** has spoken to you, remnant of Judah: ‘Do not go to Egypt.’ Be certain of this: I have warned you today.|Separates Jeremiah's warning from the quoted divine command.

42:20|You have made a fatal mistake. You yourselves sent me to the **LORD** your God, saying, ‘Pray for us to the **LORD** our God. Tell us everything the **LORD** our God says, and we will do it.’|Reads the erring as endangering their lives; preserves all three divine names in the recalled pledge.
42:21|I have told you today, but you have not obeyed the **LORD** your God in anything he sent me to tell you.|Retains the accusation that their response has already failed the pledge.
42:22|So be certain: you will die by sword, famine, and plague in the place where you want to go and settle.”|Closes with the repeated certainty and the place they desire.

43:1|Jeremiah finished telling all the people every word of the **LORD** their God—all these words the **LORD** their God had sent him to speak to them.|Preserves the repeated completeness of the message and two divine names.

43:2|Then Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah, and all the arrogant men said to Jeremiah, “You are lying! The **LORD** our God did not send you to say, ‘Do not go to Egypt to settle there.’|Keeps Azariah distinct from 42:1 and the accusation directly in their speech.

43:3|Baruch son of Neriah is turning you against us, to hand us over to the Chaldeans so they can kill us or carry us into exile in Babylon.”|Preserves the allegation against Baruch without endorsing it as narration.

43:4|So Johanan son of Kareah, all the army commanders, and all the people refused to obey the **LORD**'s command to stay in the land of Judah.|Connects the narrator's judgment to the explicit command.

43:5|Johanan son of Kareah and all the army commanders took the whole remnant of Judah who had returned from all the nations where they had been scattered to settle in Judah:|Keeps the return from dispersion before the renewed displacement.

43:6|the men, women, children, and king's daughters—everyone Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. They also took Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah.|Preserves each group and Jeremiah and Baruch as people taken, not willing leaders.
43:7|They entered Egypt, refusing to obey the **LORD**, and reached Tahpanhes.|Keeps the journey and disobedience together.
43:8|In Tahpanhes, the word of the **LORD** came to Jeremiah:|Retains the new location of revelation.

43:9|“Take large stones and hide them in the mortar of the brickwork at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, while the men of Judah watch.|Uses brickwork for the uncertain installation, with a note, and retains public witnesses.

43:10|Tell them, ‘This is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says: I am sending for my servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. I will place his throne over these stones I have hidden, and he will spread his canopy above them.|Keeps my servant and the divine first-person action, following the read form of canopy.

43:11|He will come and strike Egypt: those destined for death, to death; those for captivity, to captivity; those for the sword, to the sword.|Preserves the threefold destiny formula rather than paraphrasing it away.

43:12|I will set fire to the temples of Egypt's gods. He will burn them and carry them away. He will wrap himself in Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment, and leave there unharmed.|Retains shifts from I to he and the garment image; temples and gods remain linked in the pronouns.
43:13|He will shatter the pillars of Beth-shemesh in Egypt and burn the temples of Egypt's gods.’”|Retains Beth-shemesh and explains its Egyptian setting in a note.

44:1|The word came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans living in Egypt—in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and the land of Pathros:|Keeps four locations; Noph is rendered by the established name Memphis.

44:2|“This is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says: You have seen all the disaster I brought on Jerusalem and all Judah's towns. Today they lie ruined, with no one living in them,|Preserves the audience's witness to the present ruins.
44:3|because of the evil they did to provoke me. They went to burn incense and serve other gods, gods unknown to them, to you, and to your ancestors.|Retains three groups in the unknown-gods formula.
44:4|Again and again I sent you all my servants the prophets, saying, ‘Please do not do this abhorrent thing that I hate.’|Expresses repeated sending naturally and keeps the urgent plea and hatred.
44:5|But they would not listen or pay attention. They would not turn from their evil and stop burning incense to other gods.|Keeps refusal to listen connected to refusal to turn.

44:6|So my wrath and anger poured out and burned in Judah's towns and Jerusalem's streets. They became ruins, a desolation, as they are today.|Retains the mixed pouring and burning images and present result.

44:7|“Now this is what the **LORD**, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, says: Why are you bringing such great harm on yourselves, cutting off man and woman, child and nursing infant from Judah, leaving yourselves no remnant?|Preserves the extended title and all four threatened groups.

44:8|Why provoke me with what your hands have made, burning incense to other gods in Egypt, where you have come to settle? You will cut yourselves off and become a curse and a disgrace among all the nations of the earth.|Unpacks the long question while retaining human agency and worldwide disgrace.

44:9|Have you forgotten the evil of your ancestors, of Judah's kings and their wives, of yourselves and your wives, done in Judah and in Jerusalem's streets?|Retains all responsible groups, resolving the singular possessive collectively with a note.

44:10|To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence. They have not followed my instruction and my statutes, which I set before you and your ancestors.|Keeps the source's third-person shift and instruction language.

44:11|“Therefore this is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says: I am setting my face against you for disaster, to cut off all Judah.|Preserves the set-face image corresponding to their determination to go to Egypt.

44:12|I will take the remnant of Judah who set their faces toward Egypt to settle there, and they will all come to an end in Egypt. They will fall by the sword and waste away in famine. From the least to the greatest, they will die by sword and famine and become an example invoked in oaths, an object of horror, a curse, and a disgrace.|Keeps the repeated totality and paired means of death without smoothing repetition.
44:13|I will call those living in Egypt to account, just as I called Jerusalem to account, by sword, famine, and plague.|Retains the parallel reckoning and full triad.

44:14|None of the remnant of Judah who have come to settle in Egypt will escape or survive to return to Judah, where they long to return and live. They will not return—except for a few fugitives.”|Preserves the exception after the sweeping denial instead of harmonizing it away.

44:15|Then all the men who knew their wives were burning incense to other gods, all the women standing there—a large assembly—and all the people living in Pathros in Egypt answered Jeremiah:|Keeps men's knowledge, women's participation, and the assembly's size.
44:16|“As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the **LORD**, we will not listen to you.|Retains the direct refusal of the named divine message.

44:17|We will certainly do everything we have promised: burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we, our ancestors, our kings, and our officials did in Judah's towns and Jerusalem's streets. Then we had plenty of bread, lived well, and saw no disaster.|Preserves the people's explanation of past prosperity as their own claim.

44:18|But ever since we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and been consumed by sword and famine.”|Retains the contrasting causal account without narrator endorsement.

44:19|The women added, “When we burned incense to the Queen of Heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, did we make cakes bearing her image and pour out offerings without our husbands?”|Identifies the speakers from our husbands; records the uncertain image-making expression in a note.
44:20|Jeremiah answered all the people—the men, the women, and everyone who had replied to him:|Preserves the comprehensive audience for the counterargument.

44:21|“The incense you burned in Judah's towns and Jerusalem's streets—you, your ancestors, your kings, your officials, and the people of the land—wasn't that what the **LORD** remembered? Didn't it come to his mind?|Keeps both rhetorical questions and all participating groups.

44:22|The **LORD** could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abhorrent things you did. That is why your land became a ruin, a horror, and a curse, without inhabitants, as it is today.|Retains the stated limit of divine endurance and its narrated result.

44:23|Because you burned incense and sinned against the **LORD**, because you did not obey the **LORD** or follow his instruction, statutes, and testimonies, this disaster has overtaken you, as you see today.”|Preserves both divine names and three kinds of instruction in the causal conclusion.
44:24|Then Jeremiah said to all the people, including all the women, “Hear the word of the **LORD**, all you people of Judah in Egypt.|Keeps the women explicitly addressed before the vow language.

44:25|This is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘You and your wives have carried out with your hands what you said with your mouths: “We will certainly fulfill our vows to burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and pour out drink offerings to her.” Go ahead, confirm your vows! Fulfill your vows!|Retains the ironic challenge, repeated vows, and mouth/hand correspondence; notes feminine verb forms.

44:26|But hear the word of the **LORD**, all Judah living in Egypt: I swear by my great name, says the **LORD**, that no one from Judah anywhere in Egypt will again invoke my name by saying, “As the Lord **GOD** lives.”|Preserves all three divine-name occurrences and the ban on the oath formula.

44:27|I am watching over them for harm, not for good. All the people of Judah in Egypt will be consumed by sword and famine until they are finished.|Keeps watching turned toward disaster and the repeated completion.

44:28|Only a few who escape the sword will return from Egypt to Judah. Then all the remnant of Judah who came to settle in Egypt will know whose word stands—mine or theirs.|Retains the few survivors and the contest between competing words.

44:29|And this will be your sign, declares the **LORD**, that I will call you to account in this place, so you may know that my words of disaster against you will certainly stand.|Keeps the sign's purpose and repeated standing of words.

44:30|This is what the **LORD** says: I am handing Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt over to his enemies, to those who seek his life, just as I handed Zedekiah king of Judah over to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, his enemy who sought his life.’”|Preserves the two kings' parallel fates and the named Pharaoh.

45:1|This is the word Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah when Baruch wrote these words on a scroll as Jeremiah dictated them, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:|Makes dictation and the earlier date explicit without rearranging the book.
45:2|“This is what the **LORD**, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch:|Retains the personally addressed oracle.

45:3|‘You said, “Woe to me!
The **LORD** has added grief to my pain.
I am worn out with groaning
and can find no rest.”’|Keeps Baruch's lament and attribution of added grief to God.

45:4|“This is what you are to tell him: ‘The **LORD** says:
What I built, I am tearing down;
what I planted, I am uprooting—
and that means the whole land.|Preserves the message-within-message and building/planting motifs.

45:5|And you seek great things for yourself?
Do not seek them.
I am bringing disaster on all flesh, declares the **LORD**.
But wherever you go, I will give you your life as plunder.’”|Retains all flesh and the recurring life-as-plunder image without inventing Baruch's ambitions.
46:1|The word of the **LORD** that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations:|Keeps the collection heading as a verse.

46:2|Concerning Egypt: the army of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, which was by the Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah.|Preserves the full battle location, rulers, and regnal date.
46:3|“Ready the small shield and the large shield!\nAdvance to battle!|Distinguishes the shield terms and retains the martial summons.

46:4|Harness the horses!
Mount up, riders!
Take your positions with helmets on.
Polish the spears;
put on your armor!|Keeps the sequence of equipment and preparation commands.

46:5|Why do I see them terrified,
falling back?
Their warriors are crushed.
They flee in panic and do not look back.
Terror on every side!” declares the **LORD**.|Retains the sudden reversal and familiar terror refrain.

46:6|The swift cannot flee;
the warrior cannot escape.
In the north, beside the Euphrates,
they stumble and fall.|Reads the prohibitive forms as the impossibility of escape in the defeat scene.
46:7|Who is this rising like the Nile,\nwhose waters surge like rivers?|Keeps the identifying question and rising-water image.

46:8|Egypt rises like the Nile,
its waters surging like rivers.
It says, “I will rise and cover the earth;
I will destroy cities and their people.”|Preserves Egypt's boast in its own voice and the repeated river image.

46:9|Charge, horses!
Race wildly, chariots!
Let the warriors march out:
Cush and Put, carrying shields,
and the Ludim, handling and drawing the bow.|Retains the named military peoples and their weapons.

46:10|But that day belongs to the Lord **GOD** of hosts,
a day of vengeance, when he takes vengeance on his enemies.
The sword will eat its fill
and drink its fill of their blood.
For the Lord **GOD** of hosts has a sacrifice
in the north, beside the Euphrates.|Keeps the repeated divine title, sword's appetite, and sacrificial violence.

46:11|Go up to Gilead and get balm,
virgin daughter Egypt!
You multiply remedies in vain;
there is no healing for you.|Preserves the personified daughter and fruitless treatment, following the feminine read form.
46:13|The word the **LORD** spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon coming to strike Egypt:|Marks a new oracle without merging it with the Carchemish heading.

46:14|“Announce it in Egypt;
proclaim it in Migdol,
proclaim it in Memphis and Tahpanhes:
‘Take your position and get ready,
for the sword has devoured all around you.’|Preserves all three local announcements and the sword's consuming action.
46:15|Why is your mighty one swept away?\nHe cannot stand,\nfor the **LORD** has driven him down.|Retains the singular verbs despite the difficult noun form and flags the mighty one in a note.

46:16|He makes many stumble;
one falls against another.
They say, ‘Get up! Let us return to our people,
to the land of our birth,
away from the oppressor's sword.’|Keeps divine causation and the foreign soldiers' return speech.
46:17|There they cry, ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt is all noise!\nHe has let the appointed time pass.’|Preserves the taunting title and missed time without supplying a specific deadline.

46:18|As I live,” declares the King,
whose name is the **LORD** of hosts,
“one is coming, like Tabor among the mountains,
like Carmel beside the sea.|Keeps the royal oath and two mountain comparisons without naming the figure beyond the context.

46:19|Pack your belongings for exile,
daughter dwelling in Egypt!
Memphis will become a desolation,
laid waste, with no one living there.|Retains exile preparations and personification.
46:20|Egypt is a beautiful heifer,\nbut a biting fly comes from the north—it comes!|Uses the biting-insect reading with uncertainty noted and preserves the doubled arrival.

46:21|Even the hired soldiers among her
are like fattened calves.
They too turn and flee together;
they do not stand.
Their day of disaster has come upon them,
the time of their reckoning.|Extends the cattle image to mercenaries and retains both time clauses.

46:22|Her sound retreats like a snake,
for they advance in force.
They come at her with axes,
like men cutting wood.|Keeps the movement of the snake-like sound and the invaders' woodcutting image.

46:23|They will cut down her forest,” declares the **LORD**,
“though it cannot be searched through.
They are more numerous than locusts,
beyond counting.|Retains the unsearchable forest and innumerable attackers without rationalizing the metaphors.
46:24|Daughter Egypt is disgraced,\nhanded over to a people from the north.”|Keeps the daughter image and transfer into another people's hand.

46:25|The **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says, “I am calling Amon of Thebes to account, along with Pharaoh, Egypt, her gods and kings—Pharaoh and everyone who trusts in him.|Preserves the repeated Pharaoh and the deity Amon; uses established Thebes for No.

46:26|I will hand them over to those who seek their lives, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his servants. Afterward Egypt will be inhabited as in former days,” declares the **LORD**.|Keeps both the handing over and the later restoration of habitation.

46:27|“But you, my servant Jacob, do not fear;
do not be dismayed, Israel.
I will save you from far away,
and your offspring from the land of their captivity.
Jacob will return and live quietly, at ease,
with no one to make him afraid.|Preserves the shift to Israel and recurring rescue language.

46:28|Do not fear, my servant Jacob,” declares the **LORD**,
“for I am with you.
I will make an end of all the nations
where I have driven you,
but I will not make an end of you.
I will discipline you justly;
I will certainly not leave you unpunished.”|Maintains the tension between preservation and punishment without minimizing either.
47:1|The word of the **LORD** that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck Gaza:|Retains the relative historical marker without assigning a date.

47:2|This is what the **LORD** says:
“Look! Waters rise from the north
and become an overflowing torrent.
They flood the land and everything in it,
the towns and those who live there.
People cry out;
everyone in the land wails.|Keeps the invading flood and its comprehensive reach.

47:3|At the pounding hooves of his stallions,
the crash of his chariots,
the roar of his wheels,
fathers do not turn back for their children;
their hands hang limp.|Preserves the fathers' failure in terror without excusing or softening it.

47:4|For the day is coming
to destroy all the Philistines,
to cut off every surviving helper
from Tyre and Sidon.
The **LORD** is destroying the Philistines,
the remnant from the coastland of Caphtor.|Keeps the named allies and origin without asserting a modern identification.

47:5|Baldness has come upon Gaza;
Ashkelon is silenced.
Remnant of their valley,
how long will you cut yourself?|Follows the pinned valley wording and preserves mourning self-injury.

47:6|Alas, sword of the **LORD**!
How long before you rest?
Return to your sheath;
be still and silent!|Retains direct appeal to the personified sword.

47:7|How can you rest,
when the **LORD** has commanded it?
Against Ashkelon and the seacoast—
there he has assigned it.”|Keeps the shift from addressing the sword to speaking about it.

48:1|Concerning Moab. This is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says:
“Woe to Nebo, for it is devastated!
Kiriathaim is disgraced and captured;
the stronghold is disgraced and shattered.|Uses stronghold for the ambiguous Misgab term, noting the possible place name.

48:2|Moab's praise is gone.
In Heshbon they plan her ruin:
‘Come, let us wipe her out as a nation.’
You too, Madmen, will fall silent;
the sword will pursue you.|Keeps the named town Madmen and the planning/silence wordplays in notes.
48:3|A cry sounds from Horonaim:\n‘Devastation! Great destruction!’|Retains the abrupt reported cry.
48:4|Moab is broken;\nher little ones raise a cry.|Follows the read form little ones instead of adopting the alternative place-name reading.

48:5|Up the slope to Luhith
they go weeping, weeping.
On the descent from Horonaim
they hear anguished cries of destruction.|Preserves uphill/downhill geography and doubled weeping; notes difficult anguish phrase.
48:6|Flee! Save your lives!\nBe like a shrub in the wilderness.|Uses the shrub reading and leaves the alternative wild-donkey interpretation in a note.

48:7|Because you trusted in your works and treasures,
you too will be captured.
Chemosh will go into exile,
his priests and officials together.|Keeps works unspecific and follows read forms for Chemosh and together.

48:8|A destroyer will come to every town;
not one town will escape.
The valley will perish
and the plateau be destroyed,
as the **LORD** has said.|Preserves the every/none repetition and two landscapes.

48:9|Give Moab wings,
for she must fly away.
Her towns will become a desolation,
with no one living in them.|Chooses the wings/flight reading of two difficult words and explicitly notes uncertainty.

48:10|Cursed is the one who does the **LORD**'s work carelessly;\ncursed is the one who holds his sword back from blood.|Keeps the violent curse intact and tied to the oracle rather than generalizing it.

48:11|Moab has been at ease since youth,
settled on its lees.
It has not been poured from vessel to vessel
or gone into exile.
So its flavor remains
and its aroma has not changed.|Preserves the sustained wine-making image and its explanation by exile.

48:12|Therefore days are coming,” declares the **LORD**,
“when I will send people to tip it out.
They will tip it out, empty its vessels,
and smash its jars.|Repeats tipping and retains vessel destruction.
48:13|Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh,\nas the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel,\nthe place it trusted.|Keeps the comparison between Moab's deity and Israel's trusted sanctuary.
48:14|How can you say, ‘We are warriors,\nmen strong in battle’?|Preserves the challenge to military self-description.

48:15|Moab is devastated;
an attacker has gone up against its towns.

51:26|No one will take from you a cornerstone\nor a stone for foundations.\nYou will be a lasting desolation,” declares the **LORD**.|Retains the two rejected building uses and permanent ruin.

51:27|Raise a signal in the land!
Blow the trumpet among the nations!
Consecrate nations against her;
summon kingdoms against her—
Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz.
Appoint a commander against her;
bring up horses like bristling locusts.|Preserves consecration, three kingdoms, and the bristling insect image.

51:28|Consecrate nations against her:\nthe kings of Media, its governors and all its deputies,\nand every land under their rule.|Keeps the repeated consecration and complete administrative reach; smooths collective pronouns minimally.

51:29|The earth shakes and writhes,
for the **LORD**'s purposes against Babylon stand:
to make Babylon's land a desolation,
with no one living there.|Keeps earth's labor-like response and the standing plan.

51:31|Runner meets runner,
messenger meets messenger,
to tell Babylon's king
that his city is captured from end to end.|Preserves the rushing repeated messengers and comprehensive capture reading.
51:32|The crossings are seized,\nthe marshes burned with fire,\nand the fighting men terrified.|Keeps marshes rather than silently substituting boats or fortifications.

51:33|For this is what the **LORD** of hosts, the God of Israel, says:
“Daughter Babylon is like a threshing floor
at the time it is trampled.
A little longer,
and her harvest time will come.”|Preserves threshing and harvest order as the image presents it.

51:34|“Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has devoured me,
crushed me, left me an empty vessel.
He swallowed me like a monster,
filled his belly with my delicacies,
then cast me away.|Follows singular read forms and keeps all bodily and vessel images.

51:35|May the violence done to me and my flesh fall on Babylon,”
says the woman dwelling in Zion.
“May my blood fall on Chaldea's inhabitants,”
says Jerusalem.|Keeps the personified woman's demand and flesh/blood parallelism.

51:36|Therefore this is what the **LORD** says:
“I will plead your case
and take vengeance for you.
I will dry up her sea
and make her spring run dry.|Preserves legal advocacy and water deprivation together.

51:37|Babylon will become heaps of rubble,
a haunt of jackals,
a horror and an object of hissing,
with no one living there.|Keeps all consequences and animal habitation.
51:38|Together they roar like young lions,\ngrowl like lion cubs.|Retains parallel animals and sounds without naming a new group.

51:39|When they are heated, I will prepare their feast
and make them drunk, so they exult.
Then they will sleep an everlasting sleep
and never wake,” declares the **LORD**.|Keeps the grotesque festive-to-death movement and ambiguous heat.
51:40|“I will bring them down like lambs to slaughter,\nlike rams with male goats.|Preserves all three animal groups and sacrificial slaughter imagery.

51:41|How Sheshach is captured,
the praise of the whole earth seized!
How Babylon has become
a horror among the nations!|Retains the cipher name and explicit Babylon parallel for the note to explain.
51:42|The sea has risen over Babylon;\nits roaring waves cover her.|Keeps the flood image without identifying a literal sea.

51:43|Her towns have become a desolation,
a dry and barren land,
a land where no one lives
and no human being passes.|Preserves both absence of settlers and passersby.

51:44|I will call Bel in Babylon to account
and pull what he swallowed from his mouth.
Nations will no longer stream to him.
Even Babylon's wall has fallen.|Connects Bel's swallowing to the earlier monster image while retaining the streaming metaphor.
51:45|Come out of her, my people!\nSave your lives, each of you,\nfrom the **LORD**'s burning anger.|Retains the personal escape command and divine wrath.

51:46|Do not lose heart or fear the reports heard in the land. One report comes one year, another the next: violence in the land, ruler against ruler.|Makes the recurring reports readable without manufacturing a timetable.

51:47|Therefore days are coming
when I will call Babylon's carved images to account.
Her whole land will be disgraced;
all her slain will fall within her.|Keeps images, land, and slain as distinct objects of judgment.

51:48|Heaven and earth and everything in them
will shout for joy over Babylon,
for destroyers will come against her from the north,”
declares the **LORD**.|Preserves cosmic rejoicing over destruction without softening its force.
51:49|Babylon must fall for Israel's slain,\njust as the slain of all the earth\nhave fallen because of Babylon.|Uses the retributive reading of the compressed clause and notes its difficulty.
51:50|You who escaped the sword, go on! Do not stand still.\nRemember the **LORD** from far away,\nand let Jerusalem come to mind.|Keeps movement, distant remembrance, and the named city.

51:51|“We are ashamed, for we have heard insults;
disgrace covers our faces.
Foreigners have entered
the holy places of the **LORD**'s house.”|Marks the community's reply and retains plural holy places.

51:52|“Therefore days are coming,” declares the **LORD**,\n“when I will call her carved images to account,\nand throughout her land the wounded will groan.|Keeps the response to the community and wounded rather than painless disappearance.
51:53|Though Babylon climbs to heaven\nand fortifies her lofty stronghold,\ndestroyers will come to her from me,” declares the **LORD**.|Retains impossible ascent and direct divine sending.
51:54|A cry sounds from Babylon,\ngreat destruction from Chaldea's land!|Keeps the brief announcement's two parallel halves.

51:55|For the **LORD** is devastating Babylon,
silencing her great voice.
Their waves roar like mighty waters;
the noise of their voices resounds.|Preserves the attackers' plural waves and voices without replacing the water image.

51:57|“I will make her officials and wise men drunk,

They will sleep an everlasting sleep
and never wake,” declares the King,
whose name is the **LORD** of hosts.|Retains the full administrative list and repeated death-sleep formula.

51:58|This is what the **LORD** of hosts says:
“Babylon's broad wall will be utterly stripped away,

Peoples labor for nothing,
nations wear themselves out for fire.”|Preserves wasted labor and fire as the outcome of building.

51:59|This is what Jeremiah the prophet instructed Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the officer responsible for resting places.|Keeps genealogy, companion journey, date, and uncertain office close to its literal wording.
51:60|Jeremiah wrote on a single scroll all the disaster that would come upon Babylon—all these words written against Babylon.|Retains the single scroll and repeated totality.
51:61|Jeremiah told Seraiah, “When you reach Babylon, see that you read all these words aloud.|Renders see and read as deliberate attention to the reading task.

51:62|Then say, ‘**LORD**, you have declared that this place will be cut off, with no one living in it, neither human nor animal. It will be a lasting desolation.’|Preserves the address, both creature groups, and duration.
51:63|When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates.|Keeps the complete symbolic action and named river.

51:64|Then say, ‘This is how Babylon will sink and never rise from the disaster I am bringing upon her. They will grow weary.’” Here end the words of Jeremiah.|Retains the awkward final weariness clause and the book's internal closing formula rather than deleting either.

52:1|Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.|Preserves ages, reign, maternal genealogy, and read name Hamutal.
52:2|He did what was evil in the **LORD**'s sight, just as Jehoiakim had done.|Keeps the evaluation and comparison with the earlier king.

52:3|Because of the **LORD**'s anger, events in Jerusalem and Judah reached the point where he cast them out of his presence. Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.|Makes the compressed causal statement readable and retains the separate rebellion notice.

52:4|In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped outside it and built siegeworks all around.|Retains the exact date and surrounding siegeworks.
52:5|The city remained under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.|Keeps duration stated by regnal year rather than calculating it.
52:6|By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was severe, and the people had no bread.|Preserves exact day/month and lack of food.

52:7|Then the city wall was breached. All the fighting men fled from the city by night through the gate between the two walls near the king's garden. With the Chaldeans surrounding the city, they took the road toward the Arabah.|Keeps the escape route and surrounding force without harmonizing a singular king into this clause.
52:8|The Chaldean army pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah on the plains of Jericho. His whole army had scattered away from him.|Preserves capture geography and abandonment.
52:9|They captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, where he pronounced judgment on him.|Keeps Riblah's region and the judicial action.
52:10|The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah's sons before his eyes. He also slaughtered all Judah's officials at Riblah.|Preserves the king's agency and repeated slaughter.

52:11|Then he blinded Zedekiah and bound him in bronze shackles. The king of Babylon took him to Babylon and kept him in custody until the day of his death.|Keeps blinding, material, destination, and lifelong confinement.

52:12|On the tenth day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, who served the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.|Preserves this date without harmonizing it to Kings.
52:13|He burned the **LORD**'s house, the king's palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. Every great house he burned with fire.|Retains the repeated burning and distinct temple/palace/houses.
52:14|The whole Chaldean army with the captain of the guard tore down Jerusalem's walls all around.|Preserves the comprehensive demolition.

52:15|Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, carried into exile some of the poor, the people remaining in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the population.|Uses population for the difficult final collective, noting the possible artisans reading.
52:16|But Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, left some of the poorest people of the land to tend vineyards and fields.|Keeps some poor deported and others left without erasing the distinction.

52:17|The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars of the **LORD**'s house, the stands, and the bronze Sea in the **LORD**'s house. They carried all their bronze to Babylon.|Retains both divine names and the named Sea vessel.
52:18|They took the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, basins, dishes, and all the bronze utensils used in service.|Preserves the full equipment list without merging items.

52:19|The captain of the guard took the bowls, firepans, basins, pots, lampstands, dishes, and pouring bowls—everything made of gold or silver.|Keeps the second overlapping list and both precious metals.

52:20|The two pillars, the one Sea, and the twelve bronze bulls under the stands, which King Solomon had made for the **LORD**'s house—the bronze in all these objects was beyond weighing.|Retains the difficult under-the-stands relation without harmonizing it; note addresses it.
52:21|Each pillar was eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits around, measured with a cord. It was hollow, with walls four fingers thick.|Keeps all dimensions and ancient units.

52:22|On top was a bronze capital five cubits high, with latticework and pomegranates all around it, all of bronze. The second pillar had the same decoration and pomegranates.|Preserves capital height, material, and matching second pillar.
52:23|There were ninety-six pomegranates facing outward; a hundred pomegranates in all surrounded the latticework.|Keeps both numbers without manufacturing a structural reconciliation.
52:24|The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three threshold keepers.|Preserves all offices and the number of keepers.

52:25|From the city he took one court official in charge of the fighting men, seven men who attended the king and were found in the city, the army commander's secretary who mustered the people of the land, and sixty men of the land found inside the city.|Keeps one/seven/sixty and distinct offices; does not harmonize seven with Kings.
52:26|Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.|Retains both taking and transfer to the named place.

52:27|The king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried into exile from its own ground.|Preserves execution and the concluding removal from ground.
52:28|These are the people Nebuchadnezzar carried into exile: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans;|Keeps the independent register's regnal year and exact number.
52:29|in Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year, 832 people from Jerusalem;|Preserves the second year and number without merging with the narrative date.

52:30|in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year, Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, carried away 745 Judeans. In all, 4,600 people.|Retains the third deportation and the source total, which equals the listed counts.

52:31|In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year he became king, lifted up Jehoiachin's head and released him from prison.|Keeps exact date, king's name, and head-lifting image with its concrete outcome.
52:32|He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the other kings with him in Babylon.|Preserves the preferential seat and kindly speech without claiming restoration to Judah's throne.
52:33|Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate regularly at the king's table for the rest of his life.|Makes the subject clear and renders eating before the king naturally.
52:34|The king of Babylon gave him a regular allowance, day by day, until his death, all the days of his life.|Retains the repeated lifelong provision that closes the book.
